messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Levi's Story

Levi was eighteen when he first came to the clinic, referred by his GP after his girlfriend had finally insisted he talk to someone. He worked as a project manager for a mid-sized construction firm in Auckland, a role that had seemed promising when he took it six months ago—steady income, responsibility, the kind of job that made him feel like he was building something. But the work had become increasingly difficult in ways he couldn't quite articulate to his boss, and he had begun to wonder if he would last much longer.

The source of his distress traced back to something he had witnessed when he was seven years old, though the memory itself remained fragmented and incomplete. What he could piece together, in halting sentences across our first sessions, was an evening at home in his parents' house in Wellington. His father had come home late, and there had been shouting—his mother's voice pitched high with fear, his father's voice low and furious. Levi remembered being in another room, remembered the sound of something breaking, remembered his mother crying. But the sequence of events, the specific words, the precise moment of violence—these remained scattered, like a photograph torn into pieces and only partially reassembled. When he tried to remember more, the terror would return unbidden, the same physical panic he had felt as a child, and he would stop trying. It was easier not to remember.

For most of his adolescence, Levi had managed. But as he grew older and began spending more time around men—at school, at university, now at work—he found himself unable to relax in their presence. Being alone with a man, particularly in a closed space, would trigger an acute sense of danger that his rational mind knew was disproportionate but his body could not ignore. His coworkers, his girlfriend's father, even his own best friend—all of them became sources of vigilant dread. At the construction site, he had started making excuses to work with female colleagues, and when he was forced to collaborate with the men on his team, he found himself watching their faces intently, searching for signs of aggression, trying to anticipate what they might do. His supervisor had noticed his reluctance to work certain shifts and had begun to question his reliability.

The triggers extended beyond proximity to men. A bicycle—he wasn't sure why, though he had a vague sense that a bicycle had been present during the incident—would make his chest tighten when he saw one. More acutely, the smell of alcohol would send him into a state of hyperalertness. At a pub with his girlfriend last month, a man had walked past them reeking of beer, and Levi had frozen, his heart racing, convinced something violent was about to happen. His girlfriend had asked if he was all right, and he had made an excuse about not feeling well.

To manage the anxiety, Levi had developed habits that seemed to help in the moment but had begun to consume his life. He smoked heavily—a pack a day now, sometimes more when he was stressed. He drank regularly, telling himself it was social, but increasingly he was drinking alone in the evenings to quiet the constant low-level vigilance that exhausted him. He had also begun experimenting with other substances, nothing he was proud of, but anything that could create a buffer between himself and the world felt necessary. More broadly, he had withdrawn from people. His friendship group had narrowed considerably; he made excuses to avoid gatherings, declined invitations, kept conversations with colleagues brief and professional. His girlfriend had become frustrated with his isolation, with his seeming inability to relax even with her, with the way he would jump at sudden noises—the kettle boiling, a door slamming—as though each sound was a threat.

At night, Levi had developed a ritual. He would check the front door lock, then the back door, then the windows in each room. Sometimes he would check them again. Sometimes three times. The checking provided a temporary sense of control, a reassurance that lasted only minutes before the anxiety would creep back and he would find himself standing at the door again, his hand on the lock.

What had finally brought him to the clinic was not a crisis but an accumulation. His girlfriend had given him an ultimatum: get help or she would leave. His work performance was deteriorating. His substance use was escalating. And most frighteningly to Levi himself, the fragmented memories seemed to be pressing harder against the edges of his consciousness, as though something was trying to break through. He was terrified of what might happen if he actually remembered the whole thing—if the disconnected pieces suddenly snapped together into a coherent, unbearable image. But he was also exhausted by the effort of keeping them apart.
